metadata.title: Simultaneous determination of two coefficients in the Riemannian hyperbolic equation from boundary measurements

extraction_notes.note: Theorem 1.4 is proved in two parts (Section 4.2 for a, end of Section 5 for q); each part is its own proof node proving the theorem. The continuation edge PP_Q->PP_A was not added: the q-part relies on the a-part through (4.26), which the \ref edge already records, not the other way round.

Section 4.2 ('End of the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient') is treated as one proof filling the section; Lemmas 4.3, 4.4 and the proof of 4.4 sit inside it as one setup step.
Section 2.1 redefines 'simple' via convex non-trapping and no conjugate points; content differs from Definition 1.3, so kept as a separate definition rather than a restated copy.

Several apparent typos in references: Lemma 4.1 cites the transport equation as (3.7) (eikonal) instead of (3.11); proof of Lemma 4.2 changes variables in (4.1) meaning (4.2); Lemmas 4.4/5.3 write A(m_1,alpha) and Lambda_{a,b}. Ref edges follow the source as written.

Literature survey sentences in Section 1.3 (Rakesh-Symes, Isakov, Sun, Montalto, Belishev-Kurylev ...) only summarize prior work and were not made nodes, except the explicitly stated gauge invariance of the DN map. Physical-motivation and WKB background paragraphs were also skipped.

Section 3.1 solves the transport equations in running text without a stated result; the derivation was split into claims (polar forms, ansatz verification, vanishing) and definitions (ansatz, explicit psi_a).
Equations (4.15), (5.9), (5.1), (5.10) repeat (4.13), (5.7), (4.1), (4.16) verbatim; recorded in also_stated_at instead of separate nodes.

nodes.name: Simple Riemannian manifold
nodes.statement: We say that the Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ (or that the metric $\mathrm{g}$) is simple in $\mathrm{M}$, if $\partial \mathrm{M}$ is strictly convex with respect to $\mathrm{g}$, and for any $x\in \mathrm{M}$, the exponential map $\exp_x:\exp_x^{-1}(\mathrm{M})\longrightarrow \mathrm{M}$ is a diffeomorphism. nodes.name: Simultaneous Hölder stability of absorption coefficient and potential
nodes.statement:
Let $(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})$ be a simple compact Riemannian manifold with boundary of dimension $n \geq 2$ such that $k^+(\mathrm{M},\mathrm{g})<1$, and let $T>\textrm{Diam}_{\mathrm{g}}(\mathrm{M})$.
There exist  $C>0$ and $\gamma\in(0,1)$ such that for any $a_1,a_2\in\mathscr{A}(m_1,\eta)$ and $q_1,q_2\in\mathscr{Q}(m_2)$ coincide near the boundary $\partial\mathrm{M}$, the following estimate holds true
\begin{equation} \norm{a_1-a_2}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{q_1-q_2}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}^\gamma
\end{equation}
where $C$ depends on $\mathrm{M}$, $m_1,m_2$, $\eta$ and $n$.

nodes.name: Gauge invariance of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
nodes.statement:
As was noted in \cite{[SU]}, the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
is invariant under a gauge transformation of the metric~$\mathrm{g}$. Namely, given a diffeomorphism $\psi:\mathrm{M}\to \mathrm{M}$ such that
$\psi|_{\partial\mathrm{M}}={\rm Id}$ one has $\Lambda_{\psi^*\mathrm{g},a,\,q}=\Lambda_{\mathrm{g},a,\,q}$
where $\psi^*\mathrm{g}$ denotes the pullback of the metric $\mathrm{g}$ under $\psi$.

nodes.name: Convex non-trapping manifold
nodes.statement:
A compact Riemannian manifold $(\mathrm{M},\, \mathrm{g})$ with boundary is called a convex non-trapping
manifold, if it satisfies two conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] the boundary $\partial \mathrm{M}$ is strictly convex, i.e., the second fundamental form of the boundary is positive definite at every
    boundary point,
    \item[(ii)] all geodesics having finite length in $\mathrm{M}$, i.e., for each $(x,\xi) \in S\mathrm{M}$, the maximal
    geodesic $\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)$ satisfying the initial conditions $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0) = x$ and $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0) = \xi$ is defined on
    a finite segment with extremities $\ell_{-}(x,\xi)$ and $\ell_{+}(x,\xi)$. We recall that a geodesic $\gamma: [a, b] \longrightarrow M$ is maximal
    if it cannot be extended to a segment $[a-\varepsilon_1, b+\varepsilon_2]$, where $\varepsilon_i \geq 0$ and $\varepsilon_1 + \varepsilon_2 > 0$.
\end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.2
nodes.statement:
\begin{itemize}
Item (1) is immediate from the relations $\ell_+(x,\lambda \xi)=\frac{1}{\lambda}\ell_+(x,\xi)$ and $\gamma_{x,\lambda \xi}(t)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(\lambda t)$ for any $\lambda>0$. Then 
$$
u(x,\lambda \xi)=\int_0^{\frac{1}{\lambda}\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(\lambda t)) dt = \frac{1}{\lambda} u(x,\xi).
 $$
Prove item (2). For $s \in \mathbb{R}$ sufficiently small, we set  $x_s=\gamma_{x,\xi}(s)$ and $\xi_s=\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s).$ Then, $\gamma_{x_s,\xi_s}(t)=\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)$ and $\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)=\tau_+(x,\xi)-s.$ So,
$$
 u(\gamma_{x,\xi}(s),\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(s))=u(x_s,\xi_s) = \int_0^{\ell_+(x_s,\xi_s)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t+s)) dt =\int_s^{\ell_+(x,\xi)}f(\gamma_{x,\xi}(t)) dt .
$$
 Differentiating with respect to $s$ and taking $s=0$, we obtain that 
 $$
 \frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^i(0)+\frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi_i}  \ddot {\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-f(x).
 $$
 Since we have $\gamma_{x,\xi}(0)=x$, $\dot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}(0)=\xi$ and $\ddot{\gamma}_{x,\xi}^{i}(0)=-\Gamma ^i_{jk}(x)\xi^j\xi^k,$ then $$\xi^i\frac{\partial u}{\partial x_i}-\Gamma^i_{jk}\xi^j\xi^k\frac{\partial u}{\partial \xi_i}= -f(x).$$ Thus we have $Hu=-f$.\\
To prove item (3), applying the operator $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}$ to the kinetic equation, we obtain $ \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} (Hu)=-\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} f= 0.$ It follows that 
$$
 0= \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} (Hu)  = \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_j (\xi^i  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_i u) dx^j  =(\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_j \xi^i ) \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_i u dx^j+\xi ^i  (\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_j \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_i u) dx^j.
$$
From (\ref{2.24}) and (\ref{2.25}), we get 
$$
0=\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u+H(\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}u).
$$
\end{itemize}
The proof is complete.

In some neighbourhood of $\partial \mathrm{M},$ the function $x \mapsto d_{\mathrm{g}}(x,\partial \mathrm{M})$ is smooth and $\partial \mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ is strictly convex for sufficiently small $\rho >0.$ The function $u$ is smooth on $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ since $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}\subset S\mathrm{M} \setminus S(\partial \mathrm{M})$.

nodes.name: Integrate over SM_rho
nodes.statement:
Integrating  (\ref{2.45}) over $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ and using the formula divergence (\ref{2.27}) and (\ref{2.28}), we find 
 \begin{align*}
 \int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle\right]\, \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= &
 -\int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \left[ \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\textrm{div}}(V)  + \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\textrm{div}}(W)\right]\, \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1} \cr =&
  -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \quad d\sigma^{2n-2} -(n-2)\int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle W, \xi \rangle \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1},
 \end{align*}
 where $\nu=\nu_{\rho}(x)$ is the unit vector of the outer normal to the boundary of $\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$.
 In view of (\ref{2.33}), we have 
 $$\langle W, \xi \rangle=\langle\xi,\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u\rangle ^2 = \vert Hu\vert ^2.$$
Hence, we obtain the equality 
\begin{equation} \int_{S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}}\left[ \vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2- \langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+(n-2) \vert Hu\vert^2 \right]  \,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,d\sigma^{2n-2}.
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Set up dominated convergence
nodes.statement:
Now, we wish pass to the limit as $\rho \rightarrow 0.$ We will apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem.  Denote by $\mathbb{\chi}_\rho$ the characteristic function of the set $S\mathrm{M}_{\rho}$ and by $p$  the projection $p : \partial S\mathrm{M} \longrightarrow  \partial S\mathrm{M}_\rho$, $p(x,\xi)=(x',\xi'),$ where $x'$ 
 is such that the geodesic $\gamma_{xx'}$ has length $\rho$ and intersects $\partial \mathrm{M}$ orthogonally at $x$ and $x'$, and $\xi'$ is obtained 
 by the parallel translation of the vector $\xi$ along $\gamma_{xx'}$. So the equality (\ref{2.46}) becomes

\end{equation}

Note that all the integrands of (\ref{2.47}) are smooth on $S\mathrm{M} \setminus \partial S \mathrm{M}$ and so, they converge towards their values almost everywhere, when $\rho \rightarrow 0$. 
Since the functions $\vert  \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert^2$ and $\vert Hu\vert ^2$  are positive and the second function satifies (\ref{2.43}), then the left side of (\ref{2.47}) converges as $\rho \rightarrow 0$.  To apply the Lebesgue dominated convergence theorem in (\ref{2.47}), it remains to prove that $\vert \langle V, \nu \rangle p_*  \vert$ is bounded by a summable function on $\partial S \mathrm{M}$ which does not depend on $\rho$.\\

\int_{S\mathrm{M}} \left[ \vert \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla} u \vert ^2-\langle R(\xi,\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u)\xi,  \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla} u\rangle+
(n-2) \vert Hu\vert ^2 \right]\,\mathrm{dv}^{2n-1}= -\int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}.
$$

nodes.name: Proof of (2.39)
nodes.statement:
Finally, It remains to prove the estimate (\ref{2.39}).  In view of the boundary condition $u=\mathcal{I} f$ on $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ and $u=0$ on $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$ we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \int_{\partial S\mathrm{M}} \langle V, \nu \rangle \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} &=\int_{\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}} \para{\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) , \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f)  \rangle\langle\xi,\nu\rangle-\langle \overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) , \xi\rangle\langle \overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}} (\mathcal{I} f) ,\nu\rangle} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2}\cr
& :=\int_{\partial_+ S\mathrm{M}} \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{I} f) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} .
 \end{align*}
where $\mathcal{Q}u$ is a quadratic form in variables $\overset{\mathrm{h}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and $\overset{\mathrm{v}}{\nabla}_{\textrm{tan}}u$ and hence, $\mathcal{Q}$ is a quadratic first-order  differential operator on the manifold $\partial_+ S \mathrm{M}$. Consequently, there exists a constant $C$ such that we have 
$$
\vert  \int_{\partial_+ S \mathrm{M}} \mathcal{Q}(\mathcal{I} f) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} \vert \leq C \Vert \mathcal{I} f \Vert ^2_{H^1(\partial_+ S \mathrm{M})}.
$$
 This completes the proof of the Theorem \ref{theorem}.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.2
nodes.statement:
Let $r(x,t;h)$ solves the following 
homogenous boundary value problem
\begin{equation} \left\{
\begin{array}{llll}
\para{\partial^2_t-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}r(x,t)=V_h (x,t)
& \textrm{in }\,\, Q,\cr
r(x,0)=\partial_tr(x,0)=0,& \textrm{in
}\,\,\mathrm{M},\cr
r(x,t)=0 & \textrm{on} \,\, \Sigma.
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
where the source term $V_h$ is given by 
\begin{equation} V_h(x,t)=-\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}\para{(\theta\psi_a)(x,t)e^{i\varphi/h}}.
\end{equation}
To prove our Lemma it would be enough to show that $r$ satisfies the estimates (\ref{3.25}).\\
By a simple computation, we have
\begin{align} -V_h (x,t)&=e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x)}\para{(\theta\psi_a)( x,t)}\cr
&\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\psi_a(x,t)\para{\partial_t\theta+\seq{d\varrho,d\theta}+\frac{\theta}{2}\Delta\varrho}( x,t)\cr
&\quad -\frac{2i}{h} e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\theta(x,t)\para{\partial_t\psi_a+\seq{d\varrho,d\psi_a}+\frac{a}{2} \psi_a}(x,t)\cr
&\quad-\frac{1}{h^2} \theta\psi_a(x,t) e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}\para{1-\abs{d\varrho}^2}.
\end{align}
Taking into account  (\ref{3.7})-(\ref{3.11}) and (\ref{3.12}), the right-hand side of (\ref{3.28}) becomes
\begin{align} V_h (x,t)&=-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}(\partial_t^2-\Delta+a(x)\partial_t+q(x))\para{(\theta\psi_a)(x,t)}
\cr &\equiv-e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}V_0(x,t).
\end{align}
Since $\theta\in\mathcal{V}(Q)$ and $\psi_a\in\mathcal{W}(Q)$ we deduce that $V_0\in H^1_0(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))$. 
Furthermore, there is a constant $C>0$, such that
\begin{equation} \norm{V_0}_{L^2(Q)}+\norm{\partial_tV_0}_{L^2(Q)}\leq C\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
By Lemma \ref{L.1.1}, we find
\begin{equation} r_h\in \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1_0(\mathrm{M}))\cap\mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})).
\end{equation}
Since the coefficients $a$ and $q$ do not depend on $t$, the function
$$
r^*_h(x,t)=\int_0^tr_h(x,s)ds,
$$
solves the mixed hyperbolic problem (\ref{3.26}) with the right side
$$
V^*_h(x,t)=\int_0^tV_h (x,s)ds=-ih\int_0^tV_0(x,s)\partial_s\para{e^{i\varphi(x,s)/h}}ds.
$$
Integrating by part with respect to $s$, we conclude that
$$
\norm{V^*_h}_{L^2(Q)}\leq Ch\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
$$
and by (\ref{1.5}), we get
\begin{eqnarray} \norm{r_h(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}=\norm{\partial_tr^*_h(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq
Ch\norm{\theta}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.

and by (\ref{1.6}), we have

\end{eqnarray}
Collecting (\ref{3.32})-(\ref{3.33}) and (\ref{3.34}) we get (\ref{3.25}).
The proof is complete.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.1
nodes.statement:
First, if $\theta_2$ satisfies (\ref{3.11}), $\psi_{a_2}$ satisfies (\ref{3.12}), and $h<h_0$, Lemma \ref{L.3.2} guarantees
the existence of a geometrical optics solution $u_2$
\begin{equation} u_2(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{2,h}(x,t),
\end{equation}
to the wave equation corresponding to the coefficients $a_2$ and $q_2$,
$$
\para{\partial^2_t-\Delta+a_2(x)\partial_t+q_2(x)}u(x,t)=0\quad \textrm{in}\,Q, \quad u(\cdot,0)=\partial_tu(\cdot,0)=0 \quad \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},
$$
where $r_{2,h}$ satisfies
\begin{gather} h^{-1}\norm{r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\partial_t r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\nabla r_{2,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)},
\\ \nonumber
r_{2,h}(x,t)=0,\quad\forall (x,t)\in\,\Sigma.
\end{gather}
Moreover
$$
u_2\in  \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M})) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})).
$$
Let us denote by $f_h$ the function
$$
f_h(x,t)=(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad  (x,t)\in\Sigma,
$$
and we consider $v$ the solution of the following non-homogenous boundary value problem
\begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{lll}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)} v=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, Q,\cr
v(x,0)=\partial_tv(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr
v(x,t)=u_2(x,t):=f_{h}(x,t), & \textrm{on}\,\, \Sigma.
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}
We let $ w=v-u_2$. Therefore, $w$ solves the following homogenous boundary value problem
$$
\left\{\begin{array}{lll}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w(x,t)=a(x)\partial_tu_2(x,t)+q(x)u_2(x,t) & \textrm{in}\,\,  Q,\cr
w(x,0)=\partial_tw(x,0)=0, & \textrm{in}\,\, \mathrm{M},\cr
w(x,t)=0, & \textrm{on}\,\,  \Sigma.
\end{array}
\right.
$$
Using the fact that  $a(x)\partial_tu_2+q(x)u_2 \in W^{1,1}(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))$ with $u_2(\cdot,0)=\partial_t u_2(\cdot,0)\equiv 0$, by Lemma \ref{L.1.1}, we deduce that
$$
w\in \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})\cap
H^1_0(\mathrm{M})).
$$
Therefore, we have constructed a special solution
  $$ 
  \mathcal{C}^2(0,T;L^2(\mathrm{M}))\cap \mathcal{C}^1(0,T;H^1(\mathrm{M})) \cap \mathcal{C}(0,T;H^2(\mathrm{M})),
  $$
to the backward wave equation
\begin{align*}
\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta-a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}u_1(x,t)&=0,  \quad (x,t) \in Q, \\
u_1(x,T)=u_1(x,T)&=0,  \quad x \in \mathrm{M},
\end{align*}
having the special form
\begin{equation} u_1(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})( t,x)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h}+r_{1,h}(x,t),
\end{equation}
which corresponds to the coefficients $-a_1$ and $q_1$, where
$r_{1,h}$ satisfies for $h<h_0$
\begin{equation} h^{-1}\norm{r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\partial_t r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}+\norm{\nabla
r_{1,h}(\cdot,t)}_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
Integrating by parts and using Green's formula (\ref{3.4}), we find
\begin{multline} \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}}\para{\partial_t^2-\Delta+a_1(x)\partial_t+q_1(x)}w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
= \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
=-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \partial_\nu w\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t.
\end{multline}
Taking (\ref{4.8}), (\ref{4.6}) into account, we deduce
\begin{multline} -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_tu_2\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t 
=\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{q_2,q_2}} f_{h}(x,t)\overline{g}_h(x,t) \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)u_2\overline{u}_1\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} \, \mathrm{d} t
\end{multline}
where $g_h$ is given by
$$
g_h(x,t)=(\theta_1\psi_{-a_1})(x,t)e^{i\varphi(x,t)/h},\quad (x,t)\in \Sigma.
$$
It follows from (\ref{4.9}), (\ref{4.6}) and (\ref{4.3}) that
\begin{multline} ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x) (\theta_2 \overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1})( x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t =\cr
\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t
-ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x) (\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(t,x)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
+\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)u_2(x,t)\overline{u}_1(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr
= \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h \para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t+\mathscr{R}_h.
\end{multline}
In view of (\ref{4.7}) and (\ref{4.4}), we have
\begin{equation} \abs{\mathscr{R}_h}\leq C\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by the trace theorem, we find
\begin{eqnarray} \bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}(f_{h}) \overline{g}_h \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t \bigg|
&\leq & \norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}} \norm{f_h}_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}\norm{g_h}_{L^2(\Sigma)}\cr
&\leq & Ch^{-3}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}
-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}.
\end{eqnarray}
The estimate (\ref{4.2}) follows easily from (\ref{4.10}), (\ref{4.11}) and (\ref{4.12}).\\
This completes the proof of the Lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4: stability of the absorption coefficient
nodes.statement:
Let us now complete the proof of the stability estimate of the absorption coefficient. 
\smallskip

We define the Poisson kernel of $B(0,1)\subset T_y \mathrm{M}_1$, i.e.,
$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\theta}^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\theta-\xi}^n},\quad \theta\in B(0,1);\,\, \xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
$$
For $0<\kappa<1$, we define $\Psi_\kappa: S_y\mathrm{M}_1\times S_y\mathrm{M}_1\to \mathbb{R}$ as
\begin{align} \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)=P(\kappa\theta,\xi).
\end{align}
We have the following Lemma (see Appendix A for the proof).
\begin{lemma} Let $\Psi_\kappa$ given by (\ref{4.16}), $\kappa \in (0,1)$. Then we have the following properties:
\begin{equation} \displaystyle 0\leq\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)\leq \frac{2}{\alpha_n(1-\kappa)^{n-1}},\quad \forall\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\xi,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
\end{equation}  
\begin{equation} \displaystyle \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) d\omega_y(\xi)=1,\quad \forall \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
\end{equation} 
\begin{equation} \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)\leq C(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}, \quad \forall\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
\end{equation}
\begin{equation} \norm{ \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\cdot)}_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)}^2\leq \frac{C}{(1-\kappa)^{n+3}}, \quad \forall \kappa\in (0,1),\,\forall\,\theta \in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}
\begin{lemma} Let $a_{i}\in \mathscr{A}(m_{1},\alpha)$, $q_i \in \mathscr{Q}(m_2)$, $i=1,\,2$. There exist $C>0,$
$\delta>0$, $\beta>0$ and $h_{0}>0$ such that 
\begin{equation} |\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)|\leq C \Big( h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h^{\beta}  \Big),\quad\forall \, (y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1,
\end{equation}
for any $h\leq h_{0}$. Here $C$ depends only on $\mathrm{M}$, $T$,
$m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $(y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1$ be a fixed and let $\Psi_\kappa$ be the positive function given by (\ref{4.16}). We extend $\mathcal{I}(a)$ by zero in $\partial_-S\mathrm{M}$, then,  we have
\begin{multline} \Big|\exp\para{-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)} -1 \Big|=\Big|
\displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[ \exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)-1  \Big]\,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
\leq\quad \Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[\exp\Big( -\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)
-\exp\Big(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big)   \Big]  \,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
 +\Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1} \Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\Big[\exp\Big(-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)  \Big)-1 \Big]
 d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|.
\end{multline}
Therefore, since we have
$$\begin{array}{lll} \Big| \!\exp\Big(
\!-\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)
\!-\!\exp\Big(\! -\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)
\! \Big) \Big|\!\!\!&\leq&\!\!\! C\Big|\displaystyle \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)-\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big|,\cr
\end{array}$$
and using the fact that
$$
\Big|\displaystyle \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)-\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\xi)\Big|\leq C \,|\theta-\xi|,
$$
 we deduce upon applying Lemma \ref{L.4.2} with $\Psi=\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\cdot)$ the following estimation
\begin{multline*}
\Big|\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)-1
\Big|\leq \cr
C\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\,|\theta-\xi|\,d\omega_y(\xi)+C\Big(
h^{-2}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h
\Big)\|\Psi_{\kappa}\|_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)}^{2}.
\end{multline*}
 On the other hand, by (\ref{4.20}) and (\ref{4.19}), we have the following inequality
$$
 \Big|\exp\Big(-\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta)\Big)-1
\Big|\leq C \,(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+C\Big(
h^{-2}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h
\Big)(1-\kappa)^{-(3+n)}.
 $$
 Selecting $(1-\kappa)$ small such that $(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}=h(1-\kappa)^{-(n+3)}$,
that is $(1-\kappa)=h^{2n/1+2n^2+6n}$, we find two constants $\delta>0$ and $\beta>0$
such that
$$\Big| \exp \Big( -\frac{1}{2}\, \mathcal{I}(a)(y,\theta) \Big)-1 \Big|\leq
C \Big[
h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+h^{\beta}
\Big].$$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5.1
nodes.statement:
From the equality (\ref{4.10}) and the expressions (\ref{4.6}) and (\ref{4.3}), it follows  that
\begin{multline} \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt = -

\cr +ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x) (\theta_2 \overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(\psi_{a_2}\psi_{-a_1})( x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\,\mathrm{d} t +ih^{-1}\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x) (\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t))\overline{r}_{1,h}e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_t(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_t r_{2,h}(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{a_1})(x,t) e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} a(x)\partial_tr_{2,h}(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr
-\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\overline{\theta}_1\psi_{-a_1})(x,t)r_{2,h}(x,t)e^{-i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\theta_2\psi_{a_2})(x,t)\overline{r}_{1,h}(x,t)e^{i\varphi/h}\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t\cr -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(r_{2,h}\overline{r}_{1,h})(x,t)\,\mathrm{dv}^{n}\mathrm{d} t .
\end{multline}
We set 
$$\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt = -\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}} \overline{g}_h\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}f_{h} \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t +\mathscr{R}'_h.$$
In view of (\ref{4.7}) and (\ref{4.4}), we have
\begin{equation} \abs{\mathscr{R}'_h}\leq C\para{h+h^{-1} \|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, by the trace theorem, we find
\begin{eqnarray} \bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\partial \mathrm{M}}\para{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}(f_{h}) \overline{g}_h \,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{n-1} \, \mathrm{d} t \bigg|
&\leq & \norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}} \norm{f_h}_{H^{1}(\Sigma)}\norm{g_h}_{L^2(\Sigma)}\cr
&\leq & Ch^{-3}\norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\Lambda_{a_1,q_1}
-\Lambda_{a_2,q_2}}.
\end{eqnarray}
Furthermore
\begin{multline} \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt = \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(1-\psi_{a}(x,t))\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt \cr + \int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)\psi_{a}(x,t)\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt
\end{multline}
and since
$$
\abs{1-\psi_a(x,t)}\leq C\norm{a}_{\mathcal{C}(\mathrm{M})}
$$
we deduce that 
 $$
 \bigg|\int_0^T\!\!\!\int_{\mathrm{M}} q(x)(\theta_2\overline{\theta}_1)(x,t)(1-\psi_{a}(x,t))\,\,\mathrm{dv}^{n} dt\bigg| \leq C\norm{a}_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})} \norm{\theta_1}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}\norm{\theta_2}_{\mathcal{V}(Q)}.$$ Combining with (\ref{5.4}), (\ref{5.5}) and (\ref{5.6}), the estimate (\ref{5.2}) follows.\\
  This completes the proof of the Lemma.

\Psi(\xi)  \,  \,

$$

\Psi(\xi)  \,  \,

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.4: stability of the electric potential
nodes.statement:
Let us now complete the proof of the stability estimate of the electric potentiel. We recall the definition of the Poisson kernel of $B(0,1)\subset T_y \mathrm{M}_1$, i-e.,
$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\theta}^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\theta-\xi}^n},\quad \theta\in B(0,1);\,\, \xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
$$
For $0<\kappa<1$, we define $\Psi_\kappa: S_y\mathrm{M}_1\times S_y\mathrm{M}_1\to \mathbb{R}$ as
\begin{align} \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)=P(\kappa\theta,\xi).
\end{align}
\begin{lemma} Let $a_{i}\in \mathscr{A}(m_1,\alpha)$, $q_i\in \mathscr{Q}(m_2)$, $i=1,\,2$. There exist $C>0,$
$\delta>0$, $\beta>0$ and $h_{0}>0$ such that 
\begin{equation} |\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)|\leq C \Big( h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},b_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},b_{1}}\|+ h^{-\delta}\|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}+h^{\beta}  \Big),\quad\forall \, (y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1,
\end{equation}
for any $h\leq h_{0}$. Here $C$ depends only on $\mathrm{M}$, $T$,
$m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
We fix $(y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ and let the positive function $\Psi_\kappa$ given by (\ref{5.10}),  we have
\begin{multline} \Big|\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)\Big|=\Big|
\displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)\,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
\leq\quad \Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)
\Big(\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)
-\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\xi)\Big)  \,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
 +\Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1} \Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\xi)
 d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|.
\end{multline}
Since we have
$$
\Big|\displaystyle \mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)-\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\xi)\Big|\leq C \,|\theta-\xi|,
$$ 
then we deduce upon applying Lemma \ref{L.5.2} with $\Psi=\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\cdot)$ that we have the following estimation
\begin{multline*}
\Big|\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)\Big|\leq C\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\,|\theta-\xi|\,d\omega_y(\xi)\cr
+C\Big(h+ h^{-1}\|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}+h^{-3}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|
\Big)\|\Psi_{\kappa}\|_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)}^{2}.
\end{multline*}
 On the other hand, by (\ref{4.20}) and (\ref{4.19}), we obtain
$$
 \Big|\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)\Big|\leq C \,(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+C\Big(
h^{-3}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+ h^{-1}\|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}+h
\Big)(1-\kappa)^{-(3+n)}.
 $$
 Take $(1-\kappa)$ small such that $(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}=h(1-\kappa)^{-(n+3)}$,
that is $(1-\kappa)=h^{2n/1+2n^2+6n}$, we find two constants $\delta>0$ and $\beta>0$
such that
$$\Big| \mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta) \Big|\leq
C \Big[
h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+ h^{-\delta}\norm{a}_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}+h^{\beta}
\Big].$$
The proof of Lemma \ref{L.5.3} is complete.
\end{proof}
Integrating the estimate (\ref{5.11}) over $\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1,$ with respect to $ \mu(y,\theta) \,  
\,\mathrm{d\sigma}^{2n-2} (y,\theta)$, then minimizing on $h$, we get 
\begin{equation} \|\mathcal{I}(q)\|_{L^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)}\leq C ( \|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+\|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})})^{\frac{\beta}{\beta+\delta}}.
\end{equation}
By interpolation inequality, we get
\begin{align} \norm{\mathcal{I}(q)}^2_{H^1(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)} & \leq C \|\mathcal{I}(q)\|_{L^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)}\|\mathcal{I}(q)\|_{H^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)} \cr 
&  \leq C \|\mathcal{I}(q)\|_{L^2(\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1)}.
\end{align}
From the Theorem \ref{theorem}, it follows that 
\begin{equation} \|q\|_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C ( \|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|+\|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})})^{\frac{\beta}{\beta+\delta}}.
\end{equation}
Using the estimate (\ref{4.26}), we conclude that
$$
\|q\|_{L^2(\mathrm{M})}\leq C  \|\Lambda_{a_{2},q_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},q_{1}}\|^{s_1},
$$ 
where $s_1 \in (0,1)$.
This completes the proof of the Theorem \ref{Th2}.

nodes.name: Lemma 5.3
nodes.statement:
\begin{lemma} Let $a_{i}\in \mathscr{A}(m_1,\alpha)$, $q_i\in \mathscr{Q}(m_2)$, $i=1,\,2$. There exist $C>0,$
$\delta>0$, $\beta>0$ and $h_{0}>0$ such that 
\begin{equation} |\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)|\leq C \Big( h^{-\delta}\|\Lambda_{a_{2},b_{2}}-\Lambda_{a_{1},b_{1}}\|+ h^{-\delta}\|a\|_{\mathcal{C}^0(\mathrm{M})}+h^{\beta}  \Big),\quad\forall \, (y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}_1,
\end{equation}
for any $h\leq h_{0}$. Here $C$ depends only on $\mathrm{M}$, $T$,
$m_{1}$ and $m_{2}$.
\end{lemma}

We fix $(y,\theta)\in\partial_+S\mathrm{M}$ and let the positive function $\Psi_\kappa$ given by (\ref{5.10}),  we have

\displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)\,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
\leq\quad \Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)
\Big(\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\theta)
-\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\xi)\Big)  \,d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|\cr
 +\Big| \displaystyle\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1} \Psi_{\kappa}(\theta,\xi)\mathcal{I}(q)(y,\xi)
 d\omega_y(\xi)\Big|.
\end{multline}

$$

C \Big[

\Big].$$
The proof of Lemma \ref{L.5.3} is complete.
\end{proof}

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement:
We define the Poisson kernel of $B(0,1)\subset T_y \mathrm{M}_1$, i-e.,
$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\theta}^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\theta-\xi}^n},\quad \theta\in B(0,1);\,\, \xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1.
$$
For $0<\kappa<1$, we define $\Psi_\kappa: S_y\mathrm{M}_1\times S_y\mathrm{M}_1\to \mathbb{R}$ as
$$
\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi)=P(\kappa\theta,\xi).
$$
Let $P_0$ the Poisson kernel for the Euclidian unit ball $B_0(0,1)\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ i.e., 
$$
P_0(\hat{\theta},\hat{\xi})=\frac{1-\abs{\hat{\theta}}_0^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\hat{\theta}-\hat{\xi}}_0^n},\quad \hat{\theta}\in B_0(0,1);\,\, \hat{\xi}\in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}.
$$
where $\abs{\cdot}_0$ is the Euclidian norm of $\mathbb{R}^n$. From the well known properties of $P_0$, we have 
$$
\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}P_0(\kappa\hat{\theta},\hat{\xi}) d\omega_0(\hat{\xi})=1, \quad\textrm{for all}\, \kappa\in (0,1),\,\, \hat{\theta}\in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}.
$$
Let $\gamma=\sqrt{\mathrm{g}}:=(\gamma_{ij})$ be definite symetric positive matrix such that $\gamma^2=(g_{ij})$, then we get
$$
P(\theta,\xi)=\frac{1-\abs{\gamma^{-1}\theta}_0^2}{\alpha_n\abs{\gamma^{-1}\theta-\gamma^{-1}\xi}_0^n},\quad \theta,\xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}.
$$
we deduce from the change of variable $\hat{\xi}=\gamma^{-1}\xi$
\begin{eqnarray} \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}P(\kappa\theta,\xi)d\omega_y(\xi)&=&\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}P_0(\kappa\gamma^{-1}\theta,\gamma^{-1}\xi)d\omega_y(\xi)\cr
&=&\frac{1}{\det\gamma}\int_{\mathbb{S}^{n-1}}P_0(\kappa\gamma^{-1}\theta,\hat{\xi})(\det\gamma) d\omega_0(\hat{\xi})=1
\end{eqnarray}
This complete the proof of (\ref{4.18}).
Let now
$$
V_\theta=\set{\xi\in S_y\mathrm{M}_1,\,\,\abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}\leq (1-\kappa)^{1/2n}}.
$$
\begin{multline} \int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)\leq\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)+(1-\kappa)\cr
\int_{V_\theta}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)+\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1\backslash V_\theta}\Psi_\kappa(\theta,\xi) \abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}d\omega_y(\xi)+(1-\kappa)\cr
(1-\kappa)^{1/2n}+4(1-\kappa)^{1/2}+(1-\kappa)\leq C(1-\kappa)^{1/2n},
\end{multline}
and then we get (\ref{4.19}).\\
By a simple computation, we have
$$
\abs{\nabla_\xi^k P(\kappa\theta,\xi)}\leq C\frac{1-\kappa^2}{\abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}^{n+k}},\quad k=1,2,
$$
we deduce that
\begin{equation}
\norm{ \Psi_\kappa(\theta,\cdot)}^2_{H^2(S_y\mathrm{M}_1)} \leq C\frac{1-\kappa^2}{(1-\kappa)^{n+4}}\int_{S_y\mathrm{M}_1}\frac{1-\kappa^2}{\abs{\kappa\theta-\xi}^n} d\omega_y(\xi)\leq 
\frac{C}{(1-\kappa)^{n+3}}.
\end{equation}
This complete the proof of (\ref{4.20}).
